patterns: is big o the actual runtime
entries.answer: Big O notation is the way of saying how a running time or memory requirement grows as the input gets larger, and it deliberately throws away constant factors so that two different implementations of the same idea can be compared. An algorithm is O of n where n is the input size when doubling the input roughly doubles the work, linear; when it takes n squared, quadratic; when the cost halves each time the input doubles, logarithmic; and when it does not depend on the input at all, constant. The letter is not a number of operations, it is a bound, and saying an algorithm is O of n log n leaves open whether the constant is 2 or 200. Dropping the constant is what makes the comparison useful and also what makes the notation wrong if you rely on it for small inputs, since a quadratic algorithm with a tiny constant can beat a linear one for a thousand elements. It is an upper bound, so O of n technically also admits something slower, and the tight form is written with theta when you have proven the bound from both sides.

entries.answer: An algorithm is a step-by-step method for solving a problem. When people compare algorithms they usually mean how the work grows as the input grows, written as Big O notation. An O(n) loop visits each item once; an O(n squared) loop compares every item to every other, so ten times the input means a hundred times the work. Choosing the right complexity is often the whole optimisation.
